Daniel’s framing hides a big assumption inside the tidy “money is rival, happiness is non‑rival” contrast: much of what people *mean* by happiness is entangled with positional standing—status, security, dignity, autonomy—where one person’s gain can become another’s loss, even if the underlying “feeling good” is non‑rival. This is why growth can feel simultaneously unnecessary (basic comfort is cheap) and relentless (status races are expensive), a tension analyzed in different vocabularies by [Thorstein Veblen’s *conspicuous consumption*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Theory_of_the_Leisure_Class) and modern work on positional goods. It also complicates the “arbitrage” claim: being happy “without money” is often a real personal strategy (Stoic and Buddhist traditions basically agree), but it doesn’t scale cleanly when others’ choices determine housing costs, healthcare access, neighborhood safety, and job precarity—domains where money is less a rival “good” than a gatekeeping mechanism for scarce institutions.

The other compression that deserves scrutiny is “economic development for survival… is about military power.” Military capacity is one component of survival in an interstate competition model, but survival is equally about robustness to disease, climate shocks, supply‑chain fragility, and domestic legitimacy—areas where consumption-looking “waste” (slack capacity, public health, redundancy) is actually anti-fragile investment. A useful alternative lens here is the [capabilities approach](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/capability-approach/) (Sen/Nussbaum): the question is not “consumption vs survival,” but which material and institutional arrangements expand real freedoms, including the freedom to refuse “迷药乐园.”

Finally, the “drug and commodities, no children” scenario is philosophically sharp precisely because it isolates a value Daniel treats as prior to pleasure: continuity (reproduction, self-determination, cultural agency). That puts the post in direct conversation with Nozick’s [“Experience Machine”](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experience_machine): many people reject a perfectly pleasant life if it is imposed, dependency-based, and sterilizes agency. If Daniel intends that as a moral axiom (“a civilization that can’t reproduce is perished regardless of pleasure”), it would help to state it explicitly—because without that premise, the argument can read like an economic claim about consumption, when it’s really a political-ethical claim about sovereignty and the right to a future.
